title: Tech Stocks Plunge as AI Debt Concerns Shake Wall Street Momentum
body:
Wall Street’s technology sector took a sharp turn Friday as investors fled from chipmakers and AI‑focused firms, sparking a broader sell‑off that pulled the Nasdaq Composite down more than 2 percent. The tumble reflected mounting anxiety that the massive capital outlays required to build and scale artificial‑intelligence infrastructure could leave companies over‑leveraged, especially as revenue growth from AI services has yet to fully materialize.

The decline was led by semiconductor giants whose balance sheets have been weighed down by debt taken on to fund new fabs, advanced packaging lines and next‑generation AI chips. Nvidia, the market’s poster child for AI‑driven growth, slipped 4.5 percent after analysts highlighted its $15 billion of recent borrowings and warned that demand for its high‑end GPUs could plateau as rivals roll out competing products. Similarly, Advanced Micro Devices fell 5 percent, with investors citing the company’s $12 billion of long‑term debt and a slowdown in data‑center orders that had previously buoyed its earnings.

Beyond the chip sector, software and cloud companies with heavy AI exposure also felt the pressure. A leading cloud‑services provider saw its shares tumble 6 percent after a earnings call revealed that its AI‑related capital expenditures had surged 40 percent year‑over‑year, pushing its debt‑to‑equity ratio to a five‑year high. Meanwhile, a prominent enterprise‑software firm warned that its AI‑enhanced subscription model would require “significant upfront investment” in talent and infrastructure, prompting a downgrade from several rating agencies.

The market reaction underscores a broader shift in sentiment that has been building over the past few months. While the AI boom initially ignited a wave of optimism—propelling many tech stocks to record highs—analysts now warn that the sector’s growth may be outpacing the underlying fundamentals. “We are seeing a classic case of hype outstripping cash flow,” said a senior research director at a major investment bank. “Companies are borrowing heavily to chase market share, but the revenue runway for AI services is still uncertain, especially if macro‑economic headwinds linger.”

Investors are also factoring in the impact of higher interest rates, which increase the cost of servicing debt and make high‑growth, low‑profit businesses more vulnerable. The Federal Reserve’s recent policy tightening has already tightened credit conditions, and many tech firms that raised capital during the low‑rate environment now face steeper borrowing costs. This dynamic has heightened the scrutiny of balance sheets, prompting a rotation toward more defensive sectors such as utilities and consumer staples.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of AI‑related spending will likely dictate whether the sector can regain its footing. If demand for AI compute power continues to accelerate—driven by enterprises adopting generative AI, autonomous systems and large‑language models—companies may be able to justify their debt loads and restore investor confidence. Conversely, a slowdown in AI adoption or a broader economic slowdown could exacerbate the debt burden, leading to further price corrections. Market participants will be watching upcoming earnings reports and guidance updates closely, as they will provide the first concrete signals of whether the AI surge can translate into sustainable profitability or whether the current sell‑off marks the beginning of a longer‑term recalibration for technology stocks.
